faq.a: Palpate just below the inguinal ligament, midway between the pubic tubercle and the anterior superior iliac spine.
faq.q: How do I locate the femoral pulse in a thin patient?

faq.a: Embryologically it expands into the right upper quadrant, reflecting its greater functional mass.
faq.q: Why is the liver’s right lobe larger than the left?

faq.a: Left upper quadrant tenderness with referred pain to the left shoulder (Kehr's sign) and guarding.
faq.q: What sign suggests splenic rupture on exam?

exam: What bedside landmarks would you use to safely insert a central line in the internal jugular vein? — Identify the sternocleidomastoid head, carotid artery pulse, and use ultrasound if available; avoid arterial puncture.

A patient with malaria presents with left upper quadrant pain and hypotension. What is your next step? — Suspect splenic rupture; perform focused exam, arrange urgent ultrasound or FAST, prepare for possible surgical intervention.
How does the anatomy of the thoracic inlet affect the presentation of a cervical rib? — It can compress the subclavian artery/nerve, causing neurovascular symptoms in the arm.

During a trauma survey, you find a bruised abdomen but no external wounds. Which organ is most likely injured given its fixed retroperitoneal position? — The duodenum (second part) is fixed and prone to perforation.
Explain why a patient with severe anemia may have a palpable spleen. — Chronic hemolysis (e.g., sickle cell) leads to splenic hyperplasia and enlargement.

What is the significance of the ‘triangle of safety’ in chest tube insertion? — It defines a safe zone bounded by the lateral edge of pectoralis major, anterior edge of latissimus dorsi, and a line superior to the nipple (5th intercostal space).
A child presents with a midline neck mass that moves with swallowing. What structure is it and what does it indicate? — Thyroid gland; suggests goitre or thyroiditis, assess for hypothyroidism.
Why is the knowledge of the lumbar plexus essential before performing a femoral nerve block? — The plexus lies within the psoas compartment; inadvertent vascular puncture can cause hematoma.
ai.title: Human Anatomy I
related: Common tropical infections and organ involvement
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: Foundational overview of the major body regions, their structures, blood and nerve supply, and clinical relevance for low‑resource settings. Emphasises bedside reasoning and common tropical pathologies.

b: Learn to locate structures by surface landmarks.
Link anatomy to common presentations on ward rounds.
sections.p: Human Anatomy I introduces the organization of the body into regions (head, neck, thorax, abdomen, pelvis, limbs) and the hierarchical relationship of organs, tissues and systems.

b: Head: skull bones, cranial fossae, major foramina.
Neck: cervical vertebrae, carotid sheath, thyroid.
Thorax: ribs, sternum, pleural cavities, heart.
Abdomen: peritoneal compartments, liver, spleen, kidneys.
Pelvis: bony ring, bladder, reproductive organs.
Limbs: bone shafts, major joints, neurovascular bundles.
sections.p: Each region is described by superficial landmarks, deep planes, and the organs they contain, using simple diagrams that can be reproduced on a bedside whiteboard.

b: Carotid artery lies medial to the sternocleidomastoid.
Liver contacts diaphragm superiorly and right kidney inferiorly.
Femoral nerve passes lateral to the femoral artery in the femoral triangle.
sections.p: Understanding what lies anterior, posterior, medial and lateral to each structure guides safe procedures and interpretation of imaging.

b: Common carotid → external carotid → facial artery for facial wounds.
Thoracic aorta → intercostal arteries → spinal cord supply.
Renal arteries arise directly from abdominal aorta.
sections.p: Key arterial trunks and venous drainage for each region, with emphasis on vessels that are often accessed in low‑resource hospitals.

b: C5‑T1 brachial plexus supplies upper limb.
Lumbosacral plexus supplies lower limb.
Vagus nerve (CN X) provides parasympathetic tone to thoraco‑abdominal viscera.
sections.p: Major peripheral nerves and their dermatomal/ myotomal distributions, essential for neurological exams and trauma assessment.

b: Lungs enable gas exchange; pleural pressure changes drive ventilation.
Kidneys filter plasma, maintain electrolytes and acid‑base balance.
Skeletal muscles generate movement and heat.
sections.p: Brief physiological role of each organ system, linking structure to function for bedside reasoning.

b: Traumatic neck injury → risk to carotid sheath structures.
Perforated duodenal ulcer → free air under diaphragm on upright X‑ray.
Malaria‑related splenomegaly → risk of splenic rupture.
sections.p: Common presentations in East African hospitals that rely on anatomical knowledge.

t.b: Identifies organomegaly, tenderness, neurovascular deficits; guides further testing.
Answers presence of free fluid or organ enlargement; if unavailable, use percussion and shifting dullness.

b: Remember ‘SCALP’ for layers over the skull: Skin, Connective tissue, Aponeurosis, Loose areolar, Pericranium.
Use ‘ABCs of the abdomen’: Aortic pulsation, Bowel sounds, Costal margins, Surface markings.
sections.p: Key points examiners love: surface landmarks, mnemonic for arterial branches, and a systematic regional exam.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of consciousness with neck trauma
Severe abdominal distension with absent bowel sounds
